analysis.one_liner: Reinstates and raises Superfund excise taxes on oil and chemical companies to pay for toxic waste cleanups.
analysis.headline: The Superfund Polluter Pays Restoration Act of 2015 was introduced in the Senate on December 14, 2015 and referred to the Finance Committee, where it never received a vote before Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would reinstate the Superfund excise tax on crude oil, raising it from 9.7 cents to 15.8 cents per barrel, and reinstate and increase taxes on dozens of hazardous chemicals. It would index those taxes to inflation, broaden the definition of crude oil to include tar sands and oil shale products, and make Superfund money available for environmental cleanup without needing a new appropriation each year. The Superfund trust fund was originally financed by these taxes but had been unfunded since they expired in 1995, leaving taxpayers to shoulder cleanup costs.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers and communities near toxic waste sites would benefit because polluting companies, rather than the general public, would again pay into the fund that finances cleanups of hazardous waste sites.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near toxic sites

how_it_helps.text: Reinstates the Hazardous Substance Superfund financing rate on crude oil at 15.8 cents per barrel and reinstate and increase taxes on hazardous chemicals, restoring a dedicated funding stream for toxic waste cleanup.
Makes Superfund money available for environmental remediation without requiring a new annual appropriation, so cleanup is not held hostage to yearly budget fights.
Indexes the oil tax rate and the $3.5 billion Superfund threshold to inflation so the fund's financing keeps pace with rising cleanup costs.
Expands the definition of crude oil to include bitumen, tar sands, and oil shale products, closing a loophole so newer sources of oil bear the same tax.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and petroleum companies and chemical manufacturers would pay the excise taxes, and some of that cost could be passed to consumers through higher fuel and product prices.

drawbacks.text: The excise taxes on oil and chemicals would raise costs for those industries, and some portion could be passed on to consumers in the form of higher prices for fuel, gasoline, and chemical-based products.
Making Superfund money available without further appropriation reduces annual congressional oversight of how the fund is spent.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit of restoring a dedicated polluter-funded cleanup fund and sparing taxpayers the cost of cleaning up private pollution outweighs the modest consumer price effects of a per-barrel and per-ton excise tax. The bill is a straightforward tax-and-spend design with few moving parts, though removing the annual appropriation step does trade some oversight for reliability.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on December 14, 2015.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance, which never acted on it.
No further action was taken, and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and chemical companies benefit because the excise taxes that would have funded toxic waste cleanup were never reinstated. Taxpayers continue to bear a larger share of Superfund cleanup costs through general appropriations instead of a polluter-paid dedicated fund.

for.name: Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to reinstate Superfund excise taxes on oil and chemical companies.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all three cosponsors were Democrats; the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where the majority party controlled the agenda, and it never advanced.

industries.note: The bill reinstates and raises an excise tax on crude oil, rising from 9.7 to 15.8 cents per barrel and extending to tar sands and oil shale products. Companies opposed the added cost and the bill stalled in committee.
The bill reinstates and increases per-ton excise taxes on dozens of hazardous chemicals. Those companies would bear a new tax cost to fund toxic waste cleanup.
